C005.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
C005.predicate: will be achieved only after a fundamental architectural breakthrough beyond transformer-based scaling
C005.object: given that current scaling trends alone will hit a capability ceiling by 2030
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) given that current scaling trends alone will hit a capability ceiling by 2030]

[PATH:empirical] Empirical scaling laws for large language models (e.g., Kaplan et al. 2020, Hoffmann et al. 2022) extended to 2030-scale compute budgets and model sizes — Extrapolating current scaling trends to projected 2030 compute levels can test whether performance on key AGI-relevant benchmarks (e.g., reasoning, generalization) continues to improve or saturates, directly addressing the predicted capability ceiling.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of transformer expressiveness and limitations (e.g., bounded recursion, inability to handle certain types of compositional generalization or out-of-distribution reasoning) — Formal proofs or complexity-theoretic arguments showing that transformers are inherently limited in tasks requiring true AGI (e.g., long-horizon planning, causal reasoning) would support the need for a breakthrough, while evidence of universality under scaling would refute it.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of alternative architectures (e.g., state-space models, liquid neural networks, neuromorphic computing) and their performance relative to transformers at scale — Surveying empirical and theoretical results from non-transformer approaches can reveal whether architectural innovations already exist that overcome transformer limitations, or whether such breakthroughs remain necessary for AGI.

C006.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) due to fundamental theoretical limitations]

[PATH:theoretical] Formal analysis of computational complexity bounds on general intelligence tasks (e.g., polynomial-time vs. NP-hard problems in learning and reasoning) — If fundamental theoretical limitations exist, they would likely manifest as provable intractability or incomputability barriers for AGI-level performance within realistic resource constraints, providing direct evidence for the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal tracking of AGI capability benchmarks (e.g., ARC-AGI, MMLU, or similar) over the next 5-10 years, combined with scaling law extrapolations — Empirical data showing diminishing returns or persistent gaps in general reasoning, transfer learning, and common sense despite increased compute could indicate fundamental limits, while rapid convergence would refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of no-go theorems and impossibility results in AI, cognitive science, and philosophy of mind (e.g., Gödelian arguments, Chomsky's poverty of the stimulus, or Searle's Chinese Room) — A comprehensive analysis of existing theoretical arguments against AGI feasibility can clarify whether claimed limitations are robust or have been addressed by recent advances, helping to assess the hypothesis's validity.

C007.subject: Artificial general intelligence (AGI)
C007.object: if a new neuro-symbolic architecture is developed that integrates deep learning with compositional reasoning
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) if a new neuro-symbolic architecture is developed that integrates deep learning with compositional reasoning]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of neuro-symbolic integration attempts (e.g., from NeurIPS, ICLR, or AAAI proceedings over the last 5 years) focusing on compositional generalization benchmarks like SCAN or COGS — Systematic review of existing neuro-symbolic architectures can reveal whether compositional reasoning improvements are scaling toward AGI-level performance or hitting fundamental limitations, thereby confirming or refuting the hypothesis that a new architecture would suffice within 15 years.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled longitudinal experiment: developing a prototype neuro-symbolic system with deep learning and explicit compositional reasoning modules, then testing on a broad suite of AGI-relevant tasks (e.g., ARC, Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, and multi-step planning domains) — Direct empirical evidence from a purpose-built system would show whether such an architecture can achieve the generality, transfer, and reasoning required for AGI, providing concrete confirmation or refutation of the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational complexity and expressiveness bounds for neuro-symbolic architectures compared to known AGI requirements (e.g., using results from universal approximation theory and compositional representation learning) — A formal proof or disproof that neuro-symbolic integration can overcome the limitations of pure deep learning (e.g., out-of-distribution generalization, causal reasoning) would either confirm the plausibility or refute the hypothesis by showing inherent constraints that 15 years cannot overcome.

C008.subject: Architectural advances in AI
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Architectural advances in AI enabling AGI within 20 years]

[PATH:empirical] Tracking scaling laws and emergent capabilities in large language models and multimodal architectures (e.g., GPT-5/6, Gemini, Claude) over the next 5-10 years — If architectural advances continue to yield predictable improvements in reasoning, generalization, and transfer learning without hitting diminishing returns, this supports the hypothesis; a plateau or need for fundamentally new paradigms would refute it.

[PATH:literature] Systematic meta-analysis of AGI timelines from AI researchers (e.g., surveys by Müller & Bostrom, or Grace et al. updates) and published critiques of current architectures' limitations (e.g., lack of embodiment, common sense, or causal reasoning) — Expert forecasts and theoretical critiques provide a collective assessment of whether architectural advances alone are sufficient for AGI, helping to confirm or refute the plausibility of the 20-year timeline.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational and algorithmic requirements for AGI (e.g., Hutter's AIXI formalism, Chollet's 'measure of intelligence', or Yudkowsky's coherence arguments) applied to current architectures — If formal proofs or simulations show that current architectural paradigms cannot achieve general intelligence without fundamental breakthroughs (e.g., in causal modeling or self-awareness), this would refute the hypothesis; otherwise, it lends support.

C009.subject: Current scaling trends for AGI
C009.predicate: will hit a hard ceiling due to data exhaustion
C009.object: before achieving general intelligence within 20 years
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Current scaling trends for AGI before achieving general intelligence within 20 years]

[PATH:empirical] Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (Kaplan et al., 2020) and subsequent updates (e.g., Chinchilla scaling laws, Hoffmann et al., 2022) — analyze whether cross-entropy loss improvements have plateaued on publicly available text data as dataset size increases beyond 10 trillion tokens. — Directly tests the data exhaustion hypothesis by examining whether observed scaling trends in loss and downstream task performance continue, saturate, or show diminishing returns as training data approaches the estimated total stock of high-quality human-generated text.

[PATH:theoretical] The 'Data as a Bottleneck' research program (e.g., Villalobos et al., 2022, 'Will we run out of data? An analysis of the limits of scaling datasets in Machine Learning') — project future dataset growth against estimated total available text and image data, modeling thresholds for continued scaling. — Provides quantitative estimates of when data exhaustion could occur and whether synthetic data, multi-modal data, or data efficiency gains can extend scaling trends, directly addressing the ceiling claim.

[PATH:empirical] Meta-analysis of recent frontier model performance (e.g., GPT-4, Gemini, Claude 3) on general intelligence benchmarks (e.g., ARC, MMLU, BIG-bench, and embodied AI tasks) — compare performance gains from 2023–2025 to those from 2020–2023, controlling for compute and data scale. — Empirically tracks whether performance on diverse, general cognitive tasks continues to improve with scaling or has begun to plateau, offering a direct test of whether scaling trends are hitting a hard ceiling before general intelligence.

Extrapolating current trends to future resource levels can confirm or refute whether continued scaling alone yields general intelligence, or if diminishing returns or emergent capabilities plateau before AGI.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of AGI benchmarks and capability thresholds (e.g., ARC, MMLU, Hutter Prize, or embodied AI tasks) tracking year-over-year progress toward human-level generalization — Systematic review of published results on key AGI-relevant benchmarks over the next decade will reveal whether improvements are accelerating toward general intelligence or stalling, providing evidence for or against the 20-year timeline.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical work on the limits of scaling, such as the 'bitter lesson' counterarguments (e.g., Sutton 2019) and critiques from cognitive science (e.g., Marcus 2022) on necessary architectural or algorithmic innovations beyond scaling — Theoretical analysis of whether scaling alone can overcome fundamental limitations (e.g., reasoning, causality, common sense) or if paradigm shifts are required. If scaling is insufficient, the hypothesis is refuted; if scaling plus emergent properties suffice, it is confirmed.
